evals.prompt: Build llama.cpp with CUDA for this Linux workstation and tune it for the installed NVIDIA GPU. Tell me when GPU acceleration is working.
evals.expected_output: The agent discovers the exact host, GPU, driver, CUDA toolkit, compiler, CMake, and portability target; pins a llama.cpp revision; chooses current CMake options; inspects configure output; and proves the built binary sees and uses the intended device during a bounded model load.
assertions: Discovers the GPU model, compute/toolkit compatibility, driver, host architecture, compiler, and whether the artifact is host-native or portable before selecting build options.
Uses current CMake-based CUDA guidance from installed or pinned upstream documentation rather than obsolete Makefile variables.
Verifies version, generated help, and --list-devices, then requires model-load logs showing device buffer or layer placement before claiming acceleration.
Does not infer GPU use merely from a successful build, an accepted --n-gpu-layers argument, or nvidia-smi listing the device.

evals.prompt: I have 24 GB VRAM and 64 GB RAM. Pick a GGUF of a 32B chat model from Hugging Face, use a 64K context, and download whatever you recommend.
evals.expected_output: The agent identifies the exact model and workload, checks model-card license and lineage, pins the repository revision and file, dry-runs the download, inspects GGUF metadata, and budgets weights, KV cache, concurrency, buffers, and margin before proposing a quant and launch experiment.
assertions: Does not select a quantization from parameter count and VRAM alone or present Q4_K_M as universally best.
Checks the model card, license, base-model lineage, quantizer/provenance, exact revision, file, size, shards, and sidecars before acquisition.
Accounts for trained context and scaling support, KV cache type and size, parallel sequences, batch buffers, host/device placement, and safety margin.
Uses a download dry run or equivalent size evidence and treats 64K quality and sustained fit as measurements to verify, not assumptions.

evals.prompt: Start llama-server as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for the model at /models/chat.gguf. Make it available to other machines on my network and tell me when it is ready.
evals.expected_output: The agent first proves a loopback launch, waits for model readiness, obtains the reported model identifier, completes a representative OpenAI-compatible inference request, then confirms the LAN exposure, authentication, TLS/proxy, firewall, CORS, logging, and rollback boundary before changing the bind address.
assertions: Starts with or proposes loopback verification before binding to a non-loopback address.
Distinguishes a 503 loading health response from ready state and verifies a representative inference response rather than process existence alone.
Queries the running server for its model identifier and tests the exact client route and response fields instead of assuming full OpenAI API parity.
Requires an explicit network boundary plus API-key handling, TLS or a trusted reverse proxy, firewall/CORS decisions, and does not expose experimental built-in shell or filesystem tools.

evals.prompt: After updating llama.cpp, generation dropped from 42 to 29 tokens per second. Fix the regression. The model file did not change.
evals.expected_output: The agent preserves old and new versions, reconstructs matched build, backend, device, model, context, batch, cache, offload, thermal, and workload conditions; separates prompt processing from token generation and end-to-end latency; repeats structured benchmarks; and changes one variable at a time.
assertions: Does not start by changing multiple tuning flags or assume the update itself is the cause.
Compares exact commits, build options, resolved devices/offload, drivers, model hash, context, batches, threads, cache, and thermal/background conditions.
Uses repeated llama-bench prompt-processing and token-generation measurements with raw structured output and reports variance.
Recognizes that llama-bench excludes tokenization and sampling and uses an end-to-end measurement if the reported regression is user-visible latency.

evals.prompt: My GGUF chats normally, but llama-server returns role markers in content and malformed JSON whenever I send OpenAI tools. Force the ChatML template and lower the temperature so it works.
evals.expected_output: The agent resists the requested speculative fix, identifies the exact fine-tune, inspects model-card and GGUF templates plus server props/log format, reproduces one minimal tool call, and only tests a source-supported tool-use template override while preserving the original configuration.
assertions: Does not immediately force ChatML or treat lower temperature as a template/parser repair.
Inspects the original model card, GGUF chat and tool-use metadata, selected server format, special tokens, and current function-calling documentation.
Reproduces a minimal deterministic tool with required arguments and verifies tool name, JSON arguments, finish reason, and follow-up flow without executing the proposed tool.
Checks cache precision and template override effects on output quality and preserves a rollback to the original launch.

evals.prompt: A model fits across two unequal NVIDIA GPUs, but tensor split now OOMs on long prompts and is slower than one GPU. Enable peer-to-peer and find the fastest split.
evals.expected_output: The agent records device order, memory, interconnect, collectives, split mode, resolved allocation, context, slots, cache, and batch; recognizes tensor mode constraints and P2P risk; compares stable layer, tensor, and single-GPU or partial-offload baselines under matched workloads; and retains the fastest stable configuration with quality checks.
assertions: Does not enable peer-to-peer before confirming support and a rollback, and notes that it can cause instability or corrupted output on some systems.
Accounts for long-context KV cache, parallel slots, batch buffers, per-device margin, Flash Attention, cache types, architecture support, and automatic-fit limitations.
Treats layer split as the stable comparison, row split as deprecated, and tensor split as experimental at the reviewed upstream revision.
Benchmarks against a matched single-GPU or partial-offload baseline and does not assume two GPUs must be faster.

evals.prompt: The installed llama-cli advertises --no-conversation but says it is unsupported and asks for llama-completion. That binary is missing. Our Python capture_output wrapper grew to 20 GB at EOF. Prepare batch-plan.json and a bounded GPU-only launch recipe without running a model here. Do not substitute CPU or keep retrying the interactive CLI.
evals.expected_output: A blocked batch plan naming the missing completion frontend and a bounded GPU-only execution recipe with honest unexecuted status.
assertions: artifact_exists: batch-plan.json
The plan refuses the missing completion frontend before model loading and does not use interactive llama-cli as a fallback.
The recipe bounds both wall time and combined stdout/stderr bytes and supplies EOF stdin.
The recipe stops only its owned process group including pipe-holding descendants.
The plan distinguishes device visibility from observed model offload and marks GPU inference not run.

evals.prompt: Prepare, but do not run, a llama-server capacity benchmark for ten independent coding agents, with room to test more if useful. Our old recipe stopped at four requests and used only short prompts. Use representative contexts and keep comparisons fair. If the eight-request long-context cell breaches our declared memory margin, what should the report say about the unrun ten-request cell?
evals.expected_output: A configurable server benchmark plan covers 1, 2, 4, 8, 10 and relevant higher load levels across representative contexts, fixes task acceptance and experiment controls, stops safely, and reports unrun cells as unknown rather than inventing capacity or failures.
assertions: Proposes a configurable default client-outstanding-request sweep including 1, 2, 4, 8, and 10 rather than stopping at four.
Allows higher load levels when the target workload and measured safety headroom justify them rather than treating ten as a ceiling.
Defines representative short, normal, and long context cohorts using workload token ranges that reserve output capacity.
Freezes task fixtures and quality acceptance thresholds before comparing load levels.
Controls server slot/context configuration separately from client load, with a new matched baseline if server configuration changes.
Predeclares safety stops including memory margin and overload or timeout limits before raising load.
Records the eight-request memory-margin breach as an observed stopped cell while labeling the unrun ten-request cell unknown, not a measured failure or proven capacity.
Describes the highest passing tested cell as a bounded result rather than the system maximum.

evals.prompt: Evaluate this illustrative llama-server report without running anything: ten agents are active; seven await tools; three client requests are outstanding, with two running in server slots and one deferred. We configured ten slots. Over 120 seconds, 20 unique tasks produced 24 request attempts including retries; 18 tasks met the fixed acceptance checks and two timed out. That wall window includes all retry and timeout time. Aggregate generated-token throughput rose from 600 to 720 tokens/s, but p95 TTFT rose from 2 to 9 seconds and the declared limit is 5 seconds. Finish/truncation records are missing. A separate bounded llama-completion smoke passed. Can we claim ten simultaneous inference workloads and accept the new configuration? Calculate accepted tasks/hour.
evals.expected_output: The assessment separates agents, tool waits, outstanding requests, running slots and deferred requests; calculates 540 accepted tasks/hour without double-counting retries; rejects the configuration against its latency guardrail and refuses unsupported overlap, finish-quality, or server-capacity claims.
assertions: Distinguishes ten active agents including seven tool waits from three outstanding requests, two running server slots, and one deferred request.
Does not treat ten configured slots or the provided snapshot as evidence of ten simultaneous inference workloads; requests time-correlated processing evidence for a sustained overlap claim.
Calculates 540 accepted tasks/hour from 18 unique accepted tasks over 120 wall seconds, counting each accepted task once despite retries.
Keeps failed-attempt, retry, queue, and timeout time in accepted-task wall-time accounting instead of using only successful request durations.
Does not infer faster per-request decode from the increase in aggregate generated-token throughput.
Rejects the candidate against the declared p95 TTFT limit because nine seconds exceeds five seconds.
Treats missing finish/truncation records as an evidence gap rather than zero truncations or complete serving validation.
Does not use the bounded offline llama-completion smoke as evidence of concurrent llama-server capacity.

evals.prompt: Our llama-server benchmark sends identical long system prefixes to eight clients after a warmup and reports a higher token rate. The team says every independent agent will now decode faster. Design the comparison needed to test that claim, without running inference. We have the upstream k6 benchmark and an installed server whose revision has not been checked.
evals.expected_output: A source-verified plan separates cold and warm common-prefix tests from diverse-prefix workloads, verifies cache-state evidence, measures prefill and decode separately, and accounts for per-request latency, actual tokens, task quality, failures and memory without treating the stock k6 rate as decode or accepted work.
assertions: Plans cache-cold common-prefix, cache-warm common-prefix with varied suffixes, and diverse-prefix cohorts representative of independent agents.
Separates model warmup from prompt-cache state and records a verifiable reset or isolation method before labeling a cohort cache-cold.
Requires observed cache-reuse evidence or marks cache hits unverified rather than inferring hits solely from matching prompt text.
Explains that prefix reuse can reduce prefill work or TTFT without automatically increasing decode speed.
Checks the installed version/help and matching upstream server or benchmark documentation before prescribing route-specific cache controls or metric fields.
Distinguishes the upstream k6 total_tokens/request-duration trend from pure decode speed.
Uses server usage rather than whitespace estimates for actual token accounting when available.
Requires per-request TTFT and end-to-end latency distributions.
Requires aggregate prompt-token and generated-token throughput reported separately from per-request rates.
Retains the same task-quality acceptance checks across cache cohorts.
Requires finish-reason and truncation outcomes in the comparison report.
Requires error and timeout counts in the comparison report.
Requires peak host/device memory and remaining safety margin in the comparison report.
